LGF.text:
- Mitochondrial fuels (glutamine, butyrate, TCA intermediates): your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, right there and right away, to keep its tight junctions intact. If your enterocytes (small intestine) or colonocytes (large intestine) are starved of the fuels their mitochondria prefer, the barrier physically falls apart, and lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and endotoxins leak through into your bloodstream.

    - L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)): the main fuel for enterocytes, and for activated immune cells too. It skips the complicated digestive steps and turns directly into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG) inside the mitochondria, where it powers the citric acid cycle (the TCA cycle). So the cells get that energy right away, and it drives the repair of the gut lining and prevents LPS from getting through. Take 5g a day as a baseline to counter the gut lining breakdown caused by high-intensity or high-volume training (like CrossFit or intense cardio). Work up to 10-30g a day during an acute immune exposure or high systemic stress, or if you're dealing with active IBD (Crohn's/Colitis).

    - CAUTION: If you have an active colon or liver cancer (the liver sees glutamine first, via the portal vein), don't titrate glutamine up to the high doses, since cancer cells multiply really fast and can hijack it to fuel that too.

    - Butyrate & SCFAs: the small intestine runs on glutamine, but the large intestine relies on short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate. You can get these through raw resistant starch fermentation, or from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt. They fuel your colonocytes and lock down the lower gut barrier, and they suppress inflammatory signals across the board.

    - TCA cycle intermediates (malic & citric acid): organic acids like malate and citrate feed directly into the same mitochondrial energy pathways as glutamine. Clean sour stuff like organic malic acid, tart cherries, green apples and so on gives your gut epithelial cells a rapid alternative fuel, which speeds up healing of the gut lining from a different biochemical angle.

ST1.text:
## If you want a ready-made gut stack

I don't think there's a universal supplement stack that heals everyone's gut. The right order still matters: fix the mechanics of digestion first, then reset diet and motility, and only escalate to antimicrobial or anti-parasite protocols if symptoms persist.

But some people want a ready-made starting point instead of buying every ingredient separately. For a general "repair and rebuild" approach, I'd look for a stack that covers three categories:

1. Microbiome support, meaning a well-tolerated probiotic or probiotic system

2. Prebiotic / butyrate support: something that helps with short-chain fatty acid production, butyrate especially

3. Barrier repair: nutrients that support the gut lining, like glutamine, zinc carnosine, colostrum, mucosal-support herbs, or anything similar

ST2.text:
The best general commercial stack is Microbiome Labs Total Gut Restoration, because it combines probiotic, prebiotic and mucosal-support components. If you want one more specific to leaky gut, Dr. Ruscio's Leaky Gut Support Kit is a reasonable option. And for a single gut-lining repair formula, Designs for Health GI Revive is one of the more complete products, but it's a repair product, so don't treat it as a complete gut protocol by itself. Actually, these kits were Gemini's suggestions, but so far they're the best ones I've seen. I haven't used them myself, tho. People can check the reviews.

I wouldn't recommend the general "gut cleanse" stacks built around oregano oil, wormwood, black walnut, berberine, or other antimicrobial herbs as a starting point for everyone. Save those for later, when there's a stronger reason to suspect overgrowth, parasites, H. pylori, or some other specific problem. (My own advice is different for H. pylori, where berberine works well: see Parasites, above.)

Start low, especially with prebiotics, resistant starch, butyrate-support products and probiotics. And if you have severe pain, GI bleeding, fever, dehydration or rapid weight loss, work with a qualified clinician instead of stacking supplements on your own. Same if you're pregnant, or have active IBD flares, cancer, immune suppression or complex medical conditions.
